passage: In the school library, Preeti looked up from her book and saw Vijay at the far table with wet cheeks and a letter in his hand. Her first thought was that someone had upset him. She walked over, but kept her distance. "Hey. Are you okay? I can sit or go, whichever you like." He wiped his eyes with his sleeve and half laughed. "Sit. I'm fine. I just got the scholarship letter. I didn't think I'd get it, and I can't stop crying." Preeti smiled and pulled out the chair. She noticed her first guess was completely wrong. "Congratulations, then." "Thanks. It's odd, I'm so happy that my eyes won't stop leaking."

qa.q: Where was Vijay sitting when Preeti saw him?
qa.a: He was at the far table in the school library.

qa.q: What might Vijay be feeling, and what was Preeti's first guess?
qa.a: Vijay is relieved and very happy about the scholarship letter, while Preeti first guessed that someone had upset him.

qa.q: Why was Preeti's gentle question better than assuming?
qa.a: Tears can mean sadness, anger, stress, laughter or relief, so asking and staying present let her learn the truth.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt on finding her first guess was wrong?
qa.a: Preeti was probably surprised and then glad for Vijay, smiling and congratulating him. 🙂

grounding: A teen reads a friend's tears and guesses sadness, but tears also come from relief, so asking gently is wiser.

passage:
Hi Binita,
I want to say sorry about yesterday. When I saw you at the bus stop with tears running down your face, I decided you must be sad, and I started saying "oh no, don't cry, it'll be fine" in my softest voice. You looked at me as if I'd got it wrong. Then you told me you weren't sad at all, you were furious about the comment someone made in class, and the tears just came out. That was a completely different feeling, and my comforting had missed. Next time I'll ask what's going on before I decide. I stayed with you until the bus came, and I'm glad I did. Text me if you want to talk more.
Tenzin

qa.q: Where did Tenzin see Binita crying?
qa.a: Tenzin saw Binita at the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Binita actually feeling when the tears came?
qa.a: Binita was furious about a comment someone made in class, and the tears came out of anger, not sadness.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do next time Tenzin sees a friend crying?
qa.a: Ask gently what is going on and stay nearby, instead of deciding the cause and comforting the wrong feeling.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt on learning Binita was furious, not sad?
qa.a: Tenzin realised the comforting had missed and felt sorry for deciding too quickly, while still glad to have stayed until the bus came.

grounding: A teen reads a friend's tears as sadness, then learns they came from anger, so asking gently is wiser.

passage:
Gurpreet, you won't mind me telling this on the podcast, right? Okay. I'm Nikita, and last year I completely misread my best friend's tears.
Gurpreet opened the scholarship email in the library. She read it, and tears started pouring down her face. She put her head on the desk.
I panicked. I thought, she didn't get it. I started saying, "It's okay, there are other scholarships, you're still brilliant..."
She lifted her head. "Nikita. I got it."
She was crying because she'd been so scared for months, and her family couldn't pay the fees otherwise. It was relief. Pure relief.
I felt so silly. I'd been comforting her for the wrong thing.
Now, when someone cries, I just sit down next to them and ask, "Happy tears, sad tears, or some other tears?" And I wait.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet open the scholarship email?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: What were Gurpreet's tears actually showing?
qa.a: Gurpreet's tears showed relief after months of fear, because her family couldn't pay the fees without the scholarship.

qa.q: What does Nikita do now when someone cries?
qa.a: Nikita sits down beside them, asks gently which kind of tears they are, and waits instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt when Nikita started comforting her about failing?
qa.a: Gurpreet was probably a little confused, and maybe amused, since the news was actually good.

grounding: The spoken account shows a teenager misreading tears of relief as sadness, and learning to ask gently and stay present.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
I'm Seema, and I sit behind Wasim in history. On Tuesday Mr Rao handed back the test and said, loudly, "Wasim, did you even open the book?" A few people laughed.
Wasim didn't answer. He stared at his paper, jaw tight. Then I saw tears roll down his face. He wiped them off fast, angrily.
I didn't know what they meant. Sad? Embarrassed? Something at home?
At the bell, I waited. When the room emptied, I sat on the desk next to his. I didn't say anything for a bit.
Then I asked, "You okay? You don't have to explain."
"I'm not sad," he said through his teeth. "I'm furious. I studied for three days. He didn't even look at my answers properly."
Angry tears. I'd have guessed wrong.
"Want to ask him to recheck it? I'll come with you."
He nodded. We went to the staff room together.

qa.q: How many days had Wasim studied?
qa.a: For three days.

qa.q: What were Wasim's tears actually showing?
qa.a: Wasim's tears showed fury and frustration at being mocked when he had studied hard, not sadness.

qa.q: Which of Seema's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Staying present quietly after class and asking gently, without guessing, let Wasim explain the anger behind the tears.

qa.q: How might the classmates who laughed have read Wasim's tears?
qa.a: They might have assumed he was sad or ashamed about a bad mark, missing that he was angry.

grounding: A classmate's account shows tears caused by anger, and a friend asking gently and staying present instead of guessing.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
Tuesday: At lunch, Aadhya laughed so hard at Lakshmi's impression of the maths teacher that tears streamed down her face. She couldn't breathe. Lakshmi thought, wow, she's really crying. Then realised: laughing tears.
Thursday: Before the chemistry practical, Lakshmi found Aadhya in the corridor, eyes wet, fanning her face. Lakshmi almost made a joke. Then she stopped and asked, "Are you okay? What kind of tears?"
"Stress," Aadhya said. "I haven't slept. I keep forgetting the titration steps."
Lakshmi stayed with her and went through the steps once, quietly.
Saturday: The practical results came. Aadhya read hers and burst into tears again. Lakshmi sat down next to her and waited.
"I passed," Aadhya whispered. "I thought I'd failed for sure."
Relief tears.
Lakshmi laughed. "Three kinds of tears in one week. I'm going to start asking every time."

qa.q: What did Aadhya keep forgetting?
qa.a: The titration steps.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling in the corridor on Thursday?
qa.a: Aadhya was stressed and exhausted, not having slept, and anxious about forgetting the titration steps.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi learn to do over the week?
qa.a: To ask gently what kind of tears they were and stay present, instead of guessing or joking.

qa.q: How did Aadhya's tears on Saturday differ from Tuesday's?
qa.a: On Tuesday they were tears of laughter; on Saturday they were tears of relief at passing.

grounding: The three beats show one friend's tears coming from laughter, stress and relief, and the other learning to ask gently rather than guess.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Uday, sit. You asked what to do when your friend cried in class. Your Yogesh Chacha has a story about that. When I was sixteen, on results day, my friend Harpal came out of the school office and started crying at the bus stop, big tears, wiping them with his sleeve. I decided he had failed. So I started talking fast: "It's okay, the re-exam is easy, my cousin also failed, don't worry." He looked at me like I was mad. Finally he said, "I passed. Maths also. I was sure I would fail it." Those were relief tears, and I had given him a whole speech about failing! After that I learned. The next time I saw someone crying, a girl in my tuition class, I just sat next to her and asked, "Do you want company, or quiet?" She said she was so angry with her brother she could cry. Angry tears. See? Same water, different reasons. So ask, and stay.

qa.q: Where did Harpal start crying?
qa.a: Harpal started crying at the bus stop.

qa.q: What was young Yogesh feeling when he started talking fast?
qa.a: Yogesh felt worried and eager to comfort, sure Harpal had failed, which made him rush into reassurance instead of asking.

qa.q: Which choice in the story worked better, and why?
qa.a: With the girl at tuition, young Yogesh sat down and asked 'Do you want company, or quiet?', which let her explain the tears were anger instead of him guessing.

qa.q: What was it like for Harpal to hear the speech about failing?
qa.a: Harpal was confused, looking at Yogesh as if he were mad, because the tears were relief, not sadness.

grounding: It shows a teenager misreading a friend's tears as sadness when they were relief, and learning through an elder's story to ask gently and stay present.
